Redwood AE/SE went over recent perf numbers, discussed noise from live traffic, and agreed on a focused sweep (2k/4k/8k) plus a side-by-side streaming demo. Customer requested kernel-level configs and clearer guidance on KV/prefix caching tradeoffs for their mixed real-time/batch workload.
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-10-03 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (CTO, Harrow Analytics), Liam Chen (ML Engineer), Priya Shah (SRE)
Recording: https://recordings.fireflies.ai/ff-2025-10-03-harrow

Auto-summary (auto-generated): quick review of TTFT numbers, streaming anomalies, next sweep plan.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir from Redwood. Quick check: sound and video ok?
[00:06] Dana: Yeah, loud and clear.
[00:09] Maya: Hi all, Maya on the call — I'll drive the perf bits.
[00:13] Liam: Liam here. Busy week.
[00:15] Priya: Priya — SRE. We swapped on the infra notes.

[00:23] Samir: Cool. Agenda: 1) quick recap of last week's TTFT runs, 2) streaming behavior with KV/prefix caching, 3) kernel options and sequence-length tradeoffs, 4) next steps.

[00:38] Maya: I'll pull up the spreadsheet. We re-ran the 4k experiment and saw a P50 of ~220ms and P95 around 740ms on the dedicated pool with cutlass fused-attn plus our quant profile, but with streaming enabled the P95 jumped depending on request mix. There's some noise from client-side batching that we didn't account for.
[01:12] Liam: That P95 seems high compared to our on-prem baseline — we had P95 around 540ms with optimized kernels. Are we sure the configs matched?
[01:23] Maya: Good call. We intentionally left a couple flags at default to mimic hosted behavior — specifically dynamic batching window at 25ms which may differ from your batcher.
[01:34] Dana: The mix we run is weird — 60% short prompts, 30% 1k-ish, 10% >4k. The high tail is from those 10% long ones.
[01:46] Priya: Also clarify: our traffic bursts at top of hour, which might hit autoscale warmup. So some of the P95 is CPU+OS jitter.

[02:05] Maya: Right. For TTFT we care mostly about cold-start and first-token latency. We measured cold-start (empty KV) vs warm (prefilled KV) — cold was 320ms P50, warm down to 190ms P50. Warmup and prefix caching help a lot.
[02:28] Samir: To be explicit: when we say TTFT we're measuring from request arrival to first generated token leaving the network, including any routing overhead.
[02:37] Dana: Good. Can you remind us what kernel options you tested? You mentioned cutlass + triton earlier.
[02:44] Maya: Sure. We tested three stacks: 1) Cutlass fused-attn with int8 quant profile (our recommended), 2) Triton baseline kernels with half-precision, 3) a fallback generic path for streaming that's more memory-friendly but slower. Cutlass gave the best P50/P95 for medium sequence lengths but memory pressure at 8k is notable.
[03:10] Liam: Memory pressure — was that on a single GPU or multi-GPU sharded?
[03:14] Maya: Single-GPU runs for this week. For 8k we start swapping to the fallback or need KV offload.
[03:22] Priya: KV offload? To host memory? That would kill our latency.
[03:27] Maya: Exactly — that's the tradeoff. We can do KV-prefetching and keep critical KV on GPU for the first few layers, or we can shard across GPUs which reduces per-GPU memory but adds cross-GPU comms.
[03:41] Dana: We have tight latency SLOs for some endpoints — 99th under 1s. That makes the offload option risky.

[03:52] Samir: So recommendation from our side: run a targeted sweep at sequence lengths 2k, 4k, and 8k with cutlass fused-attn and the int8 profile, but also include a Triton variant for each. That will let us see where cutlass wins vs memory pressure region.
[04:12] Liam: Can you also include streaming toggles? We saw an odd case where streaming reduced per-token latency but increased TTFT due to extra routing overhead.
[04:22] Maya: Yes. We'll run each kernel with streaming enabled/disabled, and with prefix caching on/off.
[04:29] Samir: Note — prefix caching means we store the KV cache for common prefixes. It helps in conversational workloads. We saw a 30% drop in P50 when prefix cache hit rates were >40%.
[04:44] Dana: Our chat use-case should have a decent prefix hit rate for system prompts, but user prompts vary. We'll provide a sample of top prompts.
[04:53] Priya: We'll send the prompt histogram.

[05:00] Maya: On streaming, the tricky bit is that streaming requires flushing partial chunks; some kernels are tuned for single-shot generation which is more efficient. The streaming path sometimes disables some fused kernels to keep memory predictable. So you see a faster average token time but higher TTFT because of buffer aggregation.
[05:26] Liam: Sounds like we should measure TTFT explicitly with the same client-side flush patterns we use in prod. Otherwise numbers won't match.
[05:34] Samir: Agreed. Action: Liam to run the A/B using your production client with both flush intervals.

[05:40] Dana: Any thoughts on warm-up strategies? We can keep a small pool warm but that's costy.
[05:47] Maya: You can do a hybrid: cold scale for bulk, but keep a tiny pinned pool for latency-critical routes. Redwood Dedicated supports burst capacity — you can reserve minimal dedicated capacity to keep warm GPUs.
[06:02] Samir: That also ties into billing and reserved capacity decisions. We'll show the unit cost tradeoffs in the spreadsheet.

[06:12] Liam: About quantization — you used int8. Does it change output quality at our prompts? We need a quantitative check, not just manual eyeballing.
[06:22] Maya: Good point. We'll run a small eval set (50 prompts) through fp16 vs int8 and compute perplexity and BLEU-like similarity; we'll also surface hallucination/regression flags.
[06:33] Priya: Please include a diffs doc if generation changes noticeably.

[06:38] Samir: Competitor note: we heard OpenAI's streaming behaves differently since they control client SDK — that may bias latencies. Not a blocker but good to know.
[06:50] Dana: We also did a quick look at Anthropic's endpoints — they were consistent but cost was higher for us.

[07:00] Maya: Back to kernel specifics: cutlass fused-attn gives a big perf boost when the sequence length is moderate and the model fits in GPU. At 8k we need either more VRAM or to spill. Triton is more memory conservative but slower. The fallback streaming-friendly path keeps memory low but increases token compute.
[07:25] Liam: Is there a middle ground? Partial KV caching? Like keep first N tokens on GPU and spill rest?
[07:32] Maya: Yep. We can do selective KV retention — first 2k tokens pinned on GPU; older tokens offloaded. That often gives most of the benefit because recency matters for attention.
[07:44] Priya: Interesting. That might meet our SLO with less cost.

[07:50] Samir: For the next sweep we'll include: cutlass+int8 (pin 2k), cutlass+int8 (no pin), triton float16 (pin 2k), triton float16 (no pin), and the streaming fallback path. Each with streaming on/off and prefix cache on/off. It's a combinatorial matrix but we can parallelize runs.
[08:18] Dana: Can you estimate run-time for the whole matrix?
[08:22] Maya: If we parallelize across two GPU instances we should have results in 48 hours. Single-run time per configuration ~40-60 minutes including warmup.
[08:32] Liam: Ok. We'll prioritize the three: 2k/4k/8k lengths first.

[08:38] Samir: Logging and observability note: Maya, can you add token-level traces for one run so we can see where time is spent?
[08:45] Maya: Yep — we'll attach flamegraphs and per-token timings, including kernel time vs memcpy vs comms.

[08:52] Dana: A question on rollout strategy: if cutlass is our winner but only on certain lengths, can Redwood route requests by policy? We want short prompts to go to cutlass and long ones to Triton or multi-GPU path.
[09:05] Samir: Absolutely — Smart routing can route by estimated sequence length, or by a header tag. We can set a policy and an automatic fallback if the chosen pool is saturated.
[09:15] Priya: That helps. We'll need exact routing rules and SDK hooks.

[09:20] Maya: We'll share an example policy and the SDK code to set route hints.
[09:25] Liam: Regarding cost: what's the delta between cutlass and triton? Rough numbers?
[09:29] Maya: For your workload, cutlass with int8 reduces token compute by ~20-30% relative to triton in our runs; however, if you need extra GPUs to avoid spilling the KV, that adds infra cost. We'll put dollar-per-1M-tokens estimate in the sheet.

[09:45] Dana: One more — can we get model checksum/versions so we can reproduce exactly?
[09:50] Samir: Yes, we'll pin model hash and config in the spreadsheet.

[09:55] Maya: Quick note about the streaming demo: streaming performance is sensitive to client chunk size. If your clients flush every 50ms vs 200ms you'll see different TTFT profiles. Liam — what's your client flush interval?
[10:07] Liam: Currently 100ms for interactive UI, 250ms for mobile.
[10:11] Maya: We'll run both.

[10:15] (crosstalk)
[10:16] Priya: Sorry, question — autoscale cooldown we set to 120s, is that typical?
[10:20] Maya: We usually recommend 60-90s for interactive flows; 120s is okay but can increase cold-start frequency during spikes.

[10:28] Samir: Action recap in threads: Samir/Maya to share spreadsheet + kernel configs, Liam/Priya to run prod-like A/Bs and share histograms, Harrow to confirm SLOs.

[10:44] Dana: Any risks we missed?
[10:47] Maya: Regression on quality from int8 — we will show eval diffs. Also memory fragmentation can cause occasional GC events — we'll surface mem graphs.

[10:58] Liam: If cutlass needs multi-GPU to hit 8k without spilling, can Redwood Dedicated handle cross-GPU KV?
[11:04] Samir: Yes, we support sharded KV with NCCL comms, but that adds a small latency overhead. We'll quantify it.

[11:14] Dana: Great. Let's aim for the sweep and then a short call to review results. Can we do next Thursday?
[11:20] Samir: We'll aim to have results by Wednesday EOD, so Thu review works.

[11:26] Maya: I'll schedule a 30m review on 2025-10-09 10:00 PT.

[11:31] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[11:33] Samir: Thanks — we'll follow up with artifacts.

[11:36] End of recording.

Notes: transcription contains some imperfect words (triton sometimes spelled tritton by auto-transcriber), proper nouns may be mis-typed. References: benchmark spreadsheet (link to be provided), kernel config snippets (attached by Redwood), streaming demo recording to be scheduled.
